En un mundo donde la tecnología avanza a pasos agigantados, observamos cómo los robots comienzan a asumir tareas que antes parecían imposibles. En este video, un robot masilla las juntas de los paneles de yeso, demostrando precisión y eficiencia en cada movimiento, sea real o animado, nos invita a reflexionar:  En el futuro, los robots realizarán muchos de los trabajos difíciles, repetitivos y peligrosos que hoy enfrentamos. Pero hay algo que las máquinas no pueden replicar: nuestra creatividad, nuestra ética y nuestra capacidad de soñar.Los robots serán nuestros aliados, facilitando nuestras labores y permitiéndonos enfocarnos en lo que realmente importa. Seremos nosotros quienes diseñemos, innovemos y tomemos decisiones basadas en valores humanos.Mientras los robots se encargan del trabajo arduo, nosotros, los humanos, seguiremos liderando con imaginación y corazón. Porque aunque la tecnología avance, la chispa de la humanidad nunca será reemplazada.  ¿Qué opinas sobre el futuro de la tecnología en la construcción? I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

Wooden robots are a type of robot that are made from wood rather than metal or plastic. These robots often have a more organic and natural appearance, making them stand out from their more traditional counterparts. #wooden  robots can be used for a variety of purposes, from educational and research purposes to entertainment and art. Some wooden robots are even able to move and perform tasks, using a #combination of #traditional mechanical components and cutting-edge technology. Overall, wooden robots are a #unique and interesting alternative to traditional robots, offering a new perspective on the capabilities and potential of these incredible #machines.
